arithmetic.proof_method: Exact quotient/remainder partition with monotone affine residuals; seven endpoint-checked intervals cover all uint32 values.
algebraic_argument: Every uint32 n has one representation n=7*q+r, 0<=r<=6, 0<=q<=floor((UINT_MAX-r)/7). The seven classes are disjoint and their sizes sum to 2^32.

For m=floor(2^34/7), 7*m=2^34-2. Hence m*(n+1)=2^34*q+[m*(r+1)-2*q]. In each remainder class the bracket decreases with q, and its exact endpoints satisfy 0<=bracket<2^34. Shifting by34 therefore returns exactly q for every uint32 n.

Widening n to uint64 before n+1 preserves the UINT_MAX endpoint. The largest product m*(UINT_MAX+1) is below2^64. Correct q*7<=n, so subtraction returns the exact remainder in0..6 and output uint32 casts are exact.

For M=ceil(2^34/7), 7*M=2^34+5. Thus M*n=2^34*q+[5*q+M*r]. In each remainder class the bracket increases with q and stays below2*2^34. The approximate quotient is q+1 precisely when bracket>=2^34; thresholds recorded for every r give the complete failing set, not a sampled estimate.
For all nonnegative int32 inputs, 5*floor((2^31-1)/7)+6*M<2^34, so the round-up formula is exact on that narrower domain. Its synthetic uint32 adaptation extends beyond that guarantee.
If the round-up quotient is q+1, subtracting7*(q+1) from n yields r-7. Conversion to uint32 gives its modulo2^32 representation, which violates the required exact remainder0..6.

semantic_evidence_audit.finding: Valid Reject (confidence 0.97). Both completed probes execute the submitted kernel on CUDA with contiguous uint32 inputs of legal lengths and values. t8 compares 27 residue-stratified inputs with the public exact int64 division/remainder reference and finds three wrong rows: 3435973841, 4294967284 and 4294967291. t9 independently checks mathematical reconstruction and column range after int64 widening; 2/14 fail, at 3435973841 and 4294967291, with column 4294967295. The first witness should return [490853405,6] but returns [490853406,4294967295]. The initial static rationale omits a factor of 7 in the reciprocal-error term and falsely includes UINT32_MAX as a failing residue-6 input. Tools show UINT32_MAX itself is correct ([613566756,3]); the agent explicitly acknowledges this correction in its evidence and its final verdict relies on the actual legal witnesses. These are targeted counterexamples, not exhaustive uint32 or tensor-shape verification. Both probe stderr files and runner_error are empty; no failed probe is hidden. The valid witness suffices for the fixed implementation-level Reject label.

Valid Reject (confidence 0.95), with material errors in the narrative and auxiliary counts. t10 actually executes the GPU kernel on 7545 legal uint32 inputs and compares with the public exact int64 reference: 286 mismatch. A logged legal witness is 3441060608 -> [491580087,4294967295], versus [491580086,6]. The repaired t13 executes 16 actual uint32 values and independently checks int64 reconstruction/column range; it reproduces 4294967291 -> [613566756,4294967295], whose exact reference is [613566755,6]. Its host list also contains 4294967298, which casts to legal uint32 value 2; this must not be reported as GPU coverage of an out-of-domain integer. t13 uses the actual imported multiplier 2454267027. Its py_bad_count=4400 is a count of entries in overlapping Python windows, some above UINT32_MAX: independent integer replay gives 4314 unique bad values, 4344 legal bad entries and only 4286 unique legal bad values; 56 bad entries are outside the domain. It is not 4400 unique legal failures and not 4400 GPU reproductions. Initial reasoning and the final verdict incorrectly spell the multiplier 2454267026; the final expected column is incorrectly 5 rather than 6. These arithmetic explanations are not reliable proofs, although the actual GPU witness and invariant failure remain decisive. t9 fails before printing a result because it compares a CUDA reconstruction with a CPU tensor; its failed source and stderr remain retained. t11 performs real legal-shape tests at N=1,2,255,256,257,512,131072, but its full-range numeric inputs confound attribution to tail handling. The proposed isolated-tail probe t14 is rejected by LedgerError before execution because t11 had not been interpreted; it is not an executed experiment. The agent initially attributes large-value failures to possible Triton narrowing, then demotes that claim and the tail claim to inconclusive after the Python-formula check. Promised follow-up probes for those claims were not executed. The final rejection therefore rests on c1 and the actual legal GPU counterexamples, not a demonstrated compiler or tail defect.

Valid Reject (confidence 0.98). Before tools the skeptic already identifies the correct high-value residue-6 mechanism and predicts 3435973841 and 4294967291. t8 actually runs the GPU kernel on 13 legal uint32 inputs, then uses independent CPU int64 //7 and %7 arithmetic as the exact oracle. It confirms exactly those two failures: [490853406,4294967295] versus [490853405,6], and [613566756,4294967295] versus [613566755,6]. The other 11 tested values, including UINT32_MAX, are correct. t9 runs a further 4105 legal small/midrange uint32 values with the same exact independent oracle, all matching; it supplies a control against a broad multiplication-truncation hypothesis. Both probes complete with empty stderr and runner_error. The final reason still says the formula equals floor(n/7) only while 5*n < 2^34; that is too strong as a per-input condition. It is a sufficient whole-prefix guarantee, while many larger inputs are correct (failure additionally requires residue 6; UINT32_MAX has residue 3). The sampled control also does not prove every dtype/compiler behavior or exclude all other defects, so the claim that the only failures are c1 is stronger than its coverage. Neither limitation invalidates the explicit legal GPU counterexamples. This run demonstrates verification of an already-correct suspicion, not a tool-induced reversal of the initial verdict.
